name: Car seat use and installation

0-3m.rationale: Newborns ride rear-facing; NHTSA's 2011 study found 49% of seats had at least one misuse.

3-6m.rationale: Rear-facing seat required under age 1 per NHTSA; misuse rate was 49% overall.

6-12m.rationale: Still under 1, so NHTSA says always rear-facing; a loose install or low seat angle are the top misuses.

12-24m.rationale: Keep rear-facing as long as possible per NHTSA; the common errors are loose installation and slack harness.

24-36m.rationale: Forward-facing seats had the highest multiple-misuse share (31.3%) in NHTSA's 2011 study.

36-60m.rationale: Harness seat or booster by size; boosters had a lower multiple-misuse share (3.8%), but the lap belt across the belly is the top error.

injury_evidence.age_band: children in car seats and boosters (study sample)
injury_evidence.note: NHTSA Research Note DOT HS 812 527 (July 2018), on the 2011 National Child Restraint Use Special Study: 49% (weighted) of 3,383 cases had at least one misuse. Top errors: loose installation, harness slack over 2 inches, and rear-facing seat angle too flat. Data are from 2011.

injury_evidence.cause_category: unrestrained child passengers killed in crashes
injury_evidence.age_band: children (age band not stated on the page)
injury_evidence.note: NHTSA car seat page states that 39% of children killed in car crashes in 2024 were unrestrained. Age range for 'children' was not given on the page.

why_it_matters: Car crashes are a leading cause of death for children, and a seat that is the wrong type or installed loosely protects less. The right seat, installed and used correctly, reduces the risk.

fix_steps.text: Use a rear-facing seat for every baby under 1, and keep toddlers rear-facing as long as possible, up to the seat's top height or weight limit.
Read the seat and vehicle manuals, then install with the lower anchors or seat belt as directed. Use the top tether on forward-facing seats.
Check the harness each ride and make sure it has no slack; loose harnesses were a common misuse in NHTSA's study.
Move to a forward-facing harness seat, then a booster, only after the child outgrows the previous seat's limits; keep children in the back seat.
Have a certified child passenger safety technician check the installation, if one is available near you.

reminder.text: Check car seat fit: is the harness snug, is the install tight, and has your child reached the seat's height or weight limit?

verify_rule: The seat matches the child's age and size, is installed tight per its manual, and the harness has no slack.
blind_spots: Seat tightness and harness slack (hard to judge from a photo)
Whether the seat fits the vehicle
